title: Amsterdam
hookLine: Spanish and Portuguese Jews rebuild open Jewish life in Amsterdam

lines: A GROWN MAN LEARNING HIS LETTERS.
NOW HE CAN SAY IT OUT LOUD.
cards: A grown man sits at a table with a teacher half his age, sounding out Hebrew letters like a child.

His family has carried a secret for generations: clean linen laid on the beds every Friday, a grandmother who refused pork without ever saying why. Back in Portugal, saying more could have cost them everything.
Here, in a port city of canals and warehouses, he can say it out loud. He is a Jew. Now he has to learn what that means.
Today, the city where he learns it.

teach.b: After the expulsions from Spain and Portugal, some Jewish families stayed and were baptized, by force or under heavy pressure. Some kept Jewish customs in secret, and the Inquisition hunted for exactly those signs.

teach.h: A CITY WHERE THEY COULD BE OPEN.
teach.b: Over time, some of these families slipped away, and a number reached Amsterdam, a trading city where they could live openly as Jews. Getting out was dangerous.
Arriving brought a different problem: much had been forgotten. Some had never seen a Torah scroll or heard the prayers in Hebrew.
So they rebuilt Jewish life almost from the ground up. They brought in rabbis and teachers from other communities, and founded congregations and schools. Grown men chose to be circumcised.
Prayer books and teachings were printed in Spanish and Portuguese, the languages people actually spoke, so they could find their way back.
They called themselves a nation, and governed their community with care, through elders who set rules and kept the peace. An old letter in the Tanakh fits them.

teach.h: BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.
teach.b: The prophet Jeremiah writes to Jews carried off to Babylon and tells them not to wait with their bags packed: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens. Raise families.
Seek the peace of the city where you live.
Amsterdam is that letter lived out: a new home, built on purpose, and an old faith rebuilt piece by piece by people who had nearly lost it.

how: Spanish and Portuguese Jewish congregations, including in Amsterdam, keep their own melodies and customs, and their members often tell the story of ancestors who returned to open Jewish life after living in secret.

games.q: your family kept Jewish customs in secret for generations. you've reached Amsterdam, and you can live openly. what comes first?
o: keep it secret anyway, out of habit.
find teachers and relearn what was lost.
leave Jewish life behind for good.
games.why: the community brought in rabbis and teachers, founded schools and printed books in the languages people spoke.

practice: Think of something you once had and let slip: a habit of prayer or quiet, a friendship, a language, a song your family sang.
Without judging how it slipped away, hold it for a moment and ask what one small piece of it you could pick up again. If you pray, you can ask for help in your own words.
